Six months? Oh, no, no. Not at all. I mean, if you look back six months ago, things were completely fine. Actually, six months ago would have been... what, the end of summer? Early fall? Excessively? No, no, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, I know we just touched on this a second ago, but I really don't think I have any trouble stopping once I get going. It's just about having a normal back-and-forth, you know? 

Like, take Sarah and me in the evenings. I ask her how her day was, and she tells me about her spreadsheets or if her manager, Gary, is breathing down her neck again. Gary's always moving her deadlines up at the last minute, which really isn't fair to her, and I tell her she ought to say something to HR, but she hates making waves. But the point is, when she's talking about Gary, I sit there and I listen to her. I don't just run over her words or keep babbling about my own problems. I know how to take turns. 

It was the exact same way when I was working at the center. You have to be a good listener in personal care. If Mrs. Gable is telling me all about her grandson's middle school band schedule, I'm not going to just interrupt her and start talking about myself. That’s just plain rude. You nod, you say "Oh, that's nice," you let them finish. 

I've known people who can't stop talking, though. My Uncle Bob used to be exactly like that, especially at Thanksgiving. He’d corner you right by the buffet line, usually when you were just trying to get some mashed potatoes, and he’d talk your ear off for twenty minutes straight about the carburetor on his old Ford truck. You couldn't get a word in edgewise if you tried! But I'm definitely not like Uncle Bob. I'm just... well, I'm just trying to explain things to you clearly right now. I want to make sure you have the complete picture of what's going on with me and this whole unfair administrative leave nightmare, because if I leave out a detail, how are you supposed to understand the full situation, right? I just think it's important you know the context. But if you want me to stop talking, I can absolutely stop. I don't have any problem putting a lid on it, I just like to be thorough. So, no, definitely not excessive.

Annoyed? No... no, I really try to be conscious of that sort of thing. I don't think anyone's ever been annoyed by me talking. 

It's like I was saying about Sarah—she comes home from the logistics place and she's just completely wiped out from staring at a screen all day. If I was sitting there talking a mile a minute and getting on her nerves, she would absolutely tell me. She's not shy about that sort of thing at all. Like, if I'm standing in front of the TV when she's trying to watch the Final Jeopardy clue, she'll wave her hands and say, "Hey, down in front!" So if I was babbling so much that it was bothering her, she'd definitely just tell me to put a sock in it. But she doesn't. We just have our normal talks while we eat. 

And at the center, before all this administrative leave garbage happened, nobody ever tried to cut me off or walk away from me. The residents actually love it when you take the time to talk to them. So many aides just rush in, check their vitals, drop off their trays, and rush right back out into the hallway without saying two words. But I'd actually stay and converse with them. Mrs. Gable never looked annoyed, she always looked grateful for the company. 

And the other staff, too. Like Brenda, she works the front desk on the first floor. Sometimes we'd stand there by the time clock for ten, maybe fifteen minutes just shooting the breeze about the weather or her husband's gout—he gets it really bad in his big toe around the holidays—and she never once tried to interrupt me or act like she needed to get away. We just had a good back-and-forth. 

So no, I really don't think I annoy anyone with my talking. I just... I just like to make sure I'm explaining things fully, you know? Just like I'm doing right now with you. I want to make sure I'm being completely understood because this whole situation with my job is so complicated, and if I don't give you all the details, you might get the wrong idea. But I'm definitely not annoying anyone. Nobody's getting mad at me or telling me to hush.

It's serious business, falls, you know? But I guess I took it a bit too far. I started actually acting out a whole drill right there in the middle of the room. I was pulling chairs around, setting up little obstacle courses, waving my arms everywhere to demonstrate how you're supposed to catch someone or clear the way. And the thing is... I just couldn't seem to stop. My supervisor, my coworkers, they were all telling me to sit down, saying \"Okay, we get it, please take a seat,\" but I just kept going. It was like I was on a track and I couldn't get off it until the whole scene was finished. So, my boss thought maybe I should come talk to someone about it, and here I am.\n\nDoctor: Did you find yourself thinking about fall-prevention protocols repeatedly before that meeting?\n\nPatient: No, not really. I mean, it's not like I was sitting at home obsessing over it or anything. It's just... well, fall prevention is part of the job, right? You always have to have it in the back of your mind when you're working with the elderly. You're always scanning the room, looking for loose rugs, making sure their walkers are within reach, checking if their shoes have good grip. It's second nature. But before the meeting? No, I wasn't dwelling on it. I was just going about my day, making my breakfast—I usually have oatmeal with a little brown sugar, sometimes some raisins if I have them—and taking the bus to work. I was actually thinking more about the weather because they said it was going to rain and I didn't want my clients slipping on the wet pavement. But the protocol itself? No, it wasn't stuck in my head or anything like that. It just sort of... erupted during the meeting. Like, once they brought it up on the agenda, it just clicked, and suddenly it felt like the most urgent, life-or-death thing in the world, and I just had to make sure everyone understood exactly how to handle it, down to the very last detail. But before that? No, not really.\n\nDoctor: Did your behavior during the meeting cause any problems for you at work or in your relationships with your coworkers?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, actually, it caused a pretty big problem. It wasn't just a slap on the wrist or a \"hey, calm down\" kind of thing after the meeting ended. My supervisor pulled me into her office, and she looked really concerned, which honestly made me feel terrible because I've always prided myself on being reliable. She told me they were putting me on administrative leave from the senior center. Just like that. Paid leave, thankfully, but still... it's a shock to your system when you're told you can't come in to do the job you've been doing for years. I mean, I love my clients. Mr. Henderson relies on me for his morning walks, and Mrs. Gable won't let anyone else help her with her compression socks. So being told I can't be there... it's really been weighing on me. I've been sitting at home, just worrying constantly if I'm even going to be able to safely return to caregiving work at all. It's my livelihood, you know? \n\nAnd it's not just work, honestly. The whole thing has bled into everything else. My wife, Sarah, she's been a saint through all this, but I can tell it's taking a toll on her. I'm just... I'm not keeping up the way I used to. I'll start doing the dishes, and then I'll get sidetracked thinking about what happened, or just feeling completely drained, and the sink stays full. She's had to start reminding me about basic chores, like taking out the recycling on Tuesdays, and even my own appointments, like coming here today. I used to have all that locked down in my head. And church... well, we usually go every Sunday, and we have this little group we get coffee with afterward, but I've just been pulling back from them. I haven't gone the last two weeks. I just don't know what to say to them if they ask how work is going, and I don't want to explain the whole thing, so it's just easier to stay home. So, yeah, it's definitely caused a lot of problems, more than I ever expected from one staff meeting.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt a strong need to perform specific rituals or routines in your daily life, outside of work?\n\nPatient: Rituals? Routines? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I have my habits, sure, but everyone has habits, right? Like I mentioned earlier, the oatmeal for breakfast—that's a habit, but it's not like a ritual where I have to stir it exactly ten times counterclockwise or something. It's just breakfast. And, you know, I always make sure the front door is locked before bed. That's just common sense, especially in our neighborhood. We had a string of car break-ins a few summers ago, just kids looking for loose change mostly, but it makes you aware. So I check the lock, maybe jiggle the handle once just to be sure, but it's not a compulsion. I don't stand there doing it over and over for twenty minutes. \n\nMy wife, Sarah, she's actually the one who's more particular about routines at home. She likes the towels folded in thirds, not halves, and they have to go in the linen closet with the folded edge facing out. She says it looks neater, and I guess she's right, it does look like a hotel in there. But me? I'm pretty easygoing when it comes to that stuff. If I fold a towel in half, it's not the end of the world. I don't feel any kind of burning need to redo it or anything. \n\nEven with the caregiving stuff, the protocols I was talking about at the meeting, those are professional standards, not personal rituals. It's about keeping people safe, not some weird itch I have to scratch in my own head. When I'm at home, I'm just... well, lately I'm just sitting around worrying, like I said. But before all this, I'd just watch a little TV, maybe tinker with the lawnmower if it was acting up—it's an older Toro model, always needs a little finessing with the spark plug—or just relax on the porch. I don't have any strict routines I have to follow, no counting things, no washing my hands fifty times, nothing like that. Just a regular guy trying to get through the day, you know? Well, trying and lately failing, I suppose, given the whole administrative leave situation. But no, no rituals.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling anxious or worried about everyday things for more than six months?\n\nPatient: Six months? Oh, no, no. Not at all. I mean, if you look back six months ago, things were completely fine. Actually, six months ago would have been... what, the end of summer? Early fall? Yeah, because I remember we had the big autumn festival at the senior center, and I was helping Mr. Henderson carve this giant pumpkin—well, mostly I carved it and he just pointed to where he wanted the eyes and the teeth—and I wasn't worried about anything back then. Life was just... normal. You know? I'd get up, have my oatmeal, catch the bus, do my shift, come home to Sarah. We'd watch Jeopardy! after dinner. There wasn't this heavy cloud hanging over me like there is now. \n\nI mean, sure, everyone worries a little bit sometimes. You worry about the electric bill going up a few bucks in the winter, or if the car is going to need new brake pads before inspection time, but just normal everyday stuff that passes. It wasn't this constant, gnawing feeling in my stomach that I can't shake. That really only started recently. Just since this whole... this whole meeting disaster and being put on administrative leave. That's when the worry really kicked into high gear, because suddenly my whole livelihood is up in the air. \n\nLike I was saying before, sitting at home, watching the dishes pile up in the sink, knowing I can't go in and help Mrs. Gable with her socks or take Mr. Henderson for his walk... that's what's making me anxious right now. It's the not knowing what's going to happen with my job. But if you're asking about a long-term thing, like half a year of feeling like this about just regular everyday things? No, definitely not. Before this whole mess started, I was perfectly fine, just taking things one day at a time, enjoying the routine of it all. It's really just the shock of being told you can't do your job that sets your mind spinning, you know? Not some long-term worry.\n\nDoctor: Have you found yourself talking more than usual since the incident at the staff meeting?\n\nPatient: Talking more? Like... just talking a lot? No, I... I really don't think so. I mean, who would I even be talking to, right? With this whole administrative leave thing, I'm just stuck at the house all day by myself. \n\nWhen I was at the center, I was always talking. You have to in that line of work. You're constantly greeting the residents, asking Mrs. Gable about her grandkids—she has three, you know, two in college and one who just started middle school, plays the trombone, I think—or you're coordinating with the other aides. You're always calling down the hall, saying, \"Hey, I need a hand with this transfer,\" or \"Did someone check the thermostat in the rec room? It's freezing in there.\" So I was always using my voice, always chatting someone up or keeping the residents entertained. \n\nBut now? It's just me and a quiet house. Sarah works during the day, she does data entry for a logistics company over on the east side, so she's gone from about eight to five every day. So it's literally just me. I might have the TV on for some background noise, maybe catch some old reruns of M*A*S*H or whatever happens to be on daytime cable, but it's not like I'm sitting there having conversations with the television screen. \n\nAnd when Sarah gets home... I mean, sure, we talk about what we're going to do for supper, or I might vent a little bit about how unfair this whole situation is and how stressed I am about my job, but I'm not... I'm not just babbling at her or talking her ear off. She's tired from staring at spreadsheets all day, so I try to give her some peace. If anything, I feel like I'm probably quieter than usual overall because I'm just so stuck in my own head with all this worry about the bills and my clients. And like I said before, I'm even skipping the Sunday coffee group at church, so I'm definitely not talking to them, either. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm talking more. If anything, I'm probably losing my voice from just sitting around in silence all day.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed yourself speaking excessively or having difficulty stopping talking when you're with others?\n\nPatient: Excessively? No, no, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, I know we just touched on this a second ago, but I really don't think I have any trouble stopping once I get going. It's just about having a normal back-and-forth, you know? \n\nLike, take Sarah and me in the evenings. When she gets home from the logistics company—she’s been doing that data entry job for, gosh, it has to be going on four years now, right after they opened that big distribution warehouse over off Route 9—we just have a regular conversation. I ask her how her day was, and she tells me about her spreadsheets or if her manager, Gary, is breathing down her neck again. Gary's always moving her deadlines up at the last minute, which really isn't fair to her, and I tell her she ought to say something to HR, but she hates making waves. But the point is, when she's talking about Gary, I sit there and I listen to her. I don't just run over her words or keep babbling about my own problems. I know how to take turns. \n\nIt was the exact same way when I was working at the center. You have to be a good listener in personal care. If Mrs. Gable is telling me all about her grandson's middle school band schedule, I'm not going to just interrupt her and start talking about myself. That’s just plain rude. You nod, you say \"Oh, that's nice,\" you let them finish. \n\nI've known people who can't stop talking, though. My Uncle Bob used to be exactly like that, especially at Thanksgiving. He’d corner you right by the buffet line, usually when you were just trying to get some mashed potatoes, and he’d talk your ear off for twenty minutes straight about the carburetor on his old Ford truck. You couldn't get a word in edgewise if you tried! But I'm definitely not like Uncle Bob. I'm just... well, I'm just trying to explain things to you clearly right now. I want to make sure you have the complete picture of what's going on with me and this whole unfair administrative leave nightmare, because if I leave out a detail, how are you supposed to understand the full situation, right? I just think it's important you know the context. But if you want me to stop talking, I can absolutely stop. I don't have any problem putting a lid on it, I just like to be thorough. So, no, definitely not excessive.\n\nDoctor: Have you often found yourself talking so much that others around you seemed annoyed or tried to interrupt you?\n\nPatient: Annoyed? No... no, I really try to be conscious of that sort of thing. I don't think anyone's ever been annoyed by me talking. \n\nIt's like I was saying about Sarah—she comes home from the logistics place and she's just completely wiped out from staring at a screen all day. If I was sitting there talking a mile a minute and getting on her nerves, she would absolutely tell me. She's not shy about that sort of thing at all. Like, if I'm standing in front of the TV when she's trying to watch the Final Jeopardy clue, she'll wave her hands and say, \"Hey, down in front!\" So if I was babbling so much that it was bothering her, she'd definitely just tell me to put a sock in it. But she doesn't. We just have our normal talks while we eat. \n\nAnd at the center, before all this administrative leave garbage happened, nobody ever tried to cut me off or walk away from me. The residents actually love it when you take the time to talk to them. So many aides just rush in, check their vitals, drop off their trays, and rush right back out into the hallway without saying two words. But I'd actually stay and converse with them. Mrs. Gable never looked annoyed, she always looked grateful for the company. \n\nAnd the other staff, too. Like Brenda, she works the front desk on the first floor. Sometimes we'd stand there by the time clock for ten, maybe fifteen minutes just shooting the breeze about the weather or her husband's gout—he gets it really bad in his big toe around the holidays—and she never once tried to interrupt me or act like she needed to get away. We just had a good back-and-forth. \n\nSo no, I really don't think I annoy anyone with my talking. I just... I just like to make sure I'm explaining things fully, you know? Just like I'm doing right now with you. I want to make sure I'm being completely understood because this whole situation with my job is so complicated, and if I don't give you all the details, you might get the wrong idea. But I'm definitely not annoying anyone. Nobody's getting mad at me or telling me to hush.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. Focus? Well... yeah, actually, I really have. It’s been incredibly frustrating, to be honest with you.

And church... well, we usually go every Sunday, and we have this little group we get coffee with afterward, but I've just been pulling back from them. I haven't gone the last two weeks. I just don't know what to say to them if they ask how work is going, and I don't want to explain the whole thing, so it's just easier to stay home. So, yeah, it's definitely caused a lot of problems, more than I ever expected from one staff meeting.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt a strong need to perform specific rituals or routines in your daily life, outside of work?\n\nPatient: Rituals? Routines? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I have my habits, sure, but everyone has habits, right? Like I mentioned earlier, the oatmeal for breakfast—that's a habit, but it's not like a ritual where I have to stir it exactly ten times counterclockwise or something. It's just breakfast. And, you know, I always make sure the front door is locked before bed. That's just common sense, especially in our neighborhood. So I check the lock, maybe jiggle the handle once just to be sure, but it's not a compulsion. I don't stand there doing it over and over for twenty minutes. \n\nMy wife, Sarah, she's actually the one who's more particular about routines at home. She likes the towels folded in thirds, not halves, and they have to go in the linen closet with the folded edge facing out. She says it looks neater, and I guess she's right, it does look like a hotel in there. But me? I'm pretty easygoing when it comes to that stuff. If I fold a towel in half, it's not the end of the world. I don't feel any kind of burning need to redo it or anything. \n\nEven with the caregiving stuff, the protocols I was talking about at the meeting, those are professional standards, not personal rituals. It's about keeping people safe, not some weird itch I have to scratch in my own head. When I'm at home, I'm just... well, lately I'm just sitting around worrying, like I said. But before all this, I'd just watch a little TV, maybe tinker with the lawnmower if it was acting up—it's an older Toro model, always needs a little finessing with the spark plug—or just relax on the porch. I don't have any strict routines I have to follow, no counting things, no washing my hands fifty times, nothing like that. Just a regular guy trying to get through the day, you know? Well, trying and lately failing, I suppose, given the whole administrative leave situation. But no, no rituals.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling anxious or worried about everyday things for more than six months?\n\nPatient: Six months? Oh, no, no. Not at all. I mean, if you look back six months ago, things were completely fine. Actually, six months ago would have been... what, the end of summer? Early fall? It's the not knowing what's going to happen with my job. But if you're asking about a long-term thing, like half a year of feeling like this about just regular everyday things? No, definitely not. Before this whole mess started, I was perfectly fine, just taking things one day at a time, enjoying the routine of it all. It's just about having a normal back-and-forth, you know? \n\nLike, take Sarah and me in the evenings. Active? Restless? Well, yeah, I guess you could definitely say that. Thoughts that keep repeating? Like... like getting a song stuck in your head, or like a broken record? No, no, I don't really get anything like that. 

I mean, I have a lot of thoughts, obviously, like I was just telling you with the church health fair and the supply closet checklists and all those big ideas. But they aren't stuck. They don't just loop over and over where I can't turn them off. If anything, it's kind of the exact opposite, you know? Like I was saying earlier, my mind is jumping from the center's floor routines to the church fellowship hall to the winter coats in the hallway. It's definitely not stuck on just one single thing. 

Like, take Sarah's brother, Mike. Now he gets stuck on things. He'll come over for Sunday dinner and he'll talk about his fantasy football team for three hours straight, just completely fixated on his draft picks and whether his tight end has a sprained ankle, and you literally cannot get him to stop thinking about it or talking about it. He just stews on it while we're trying to eat the pot roast. But me? I'm not like that at all. I just like to be thorough when I'm handling a situation. 

If I'm thinking about a problem—like how that HR department still hasn't called me back about my union representation for this whole administrative leave mess—I'll think about it, sure. I'll analyze the situation, I'll maybe write down a few bullet points on that yellow legal pad so I have my facts straight for when they finally do decide to pick up the phone. But once I've got it figured out and I've made my plan, I move on. I don't just sit there in the living room agonizing over the exact same thought all afternoon. When I was a kid? No, not really. I mean, I know I was just telling you how I can't seem to focus on those HR forms right now, but back then? No, I was completely different. 

Take fourth grade, for example. I had Mrs. Higgins. But I wasn't like that at all. I could sit there just fine. I might have been daydreaming a little bit, sure, looking out the window at the swing sets or thinking about what I was going to do when I got home—we had this big dirt hill behind our house where my older brother and I would take our bikes and try to build these ramps out of scrap wood we found behind the hardware store—but I wasn't restless. I didn't have a motor running back then. 

I paid attention when I needed to. I could sit at my desk, do my spelling worksheets, listen to the teacher talk about state capitals... I didn't have any trouble focusing as a child. I mean, I ended up leaving high school in the tenth grade, but that wasn't because I couldn't sit still or pay attention to the chalkboard. I just kind of lost interest in the whole school thing and wanted to get out and start working and making my own money. But as a young kid? No, I was totally fine. It's really just recently, with all this ridiculous stress from the center and being stuck at home on leave, that my brain feels like it's ping-ponging all over the place. Back then, I could sit still for hours if I had to.

Always talked this much? No, no way. Definitely not. I mean, if you asked Sarah, she’d probably tell you I’m usually the quiet one in the house. Anxiety? Discomfort? No, no, it's not like that at all.
